name: SeaweedFS
vendor: Chris Lu and contributors; a paid Enterprise edition is sold at seaweedfs.com
summary: A distributed blob store with an S3 gateway and a file system layer, built to store and serve billions of small files.
intro: SeaweedFS splits storage into three roles. Volume servers pack many files into large append-only volume files and keep a 16-byte index entry per file in memory, so reading any file, small or large, takes one disk seek. Master servers (one, or three in a Raft group) track volumes, not files: clients ask a master which server holds a volume, cache the answer and then talk to volume servers directly. Copies are made per volume with a three-digit setting for data centre, rack and server, so `001` means one extra copy on another server and `010` one on another rack. Volumes that have gone warm can later be converted to Reed-Solomon 10+4 erasure coding in the background.

On top sits the filer, which adds directories and file names and keeps that metadata in a database you choose: embedded LevelDB by default, or PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis, Cassandra, TiKV and many others. The S3 gateway, WebDAV, SFTP, a FUSE mount and a Kubernetes CSI driver all go through the filer, so the same data is reachable as S3 objects and as files. The S3 gateway covers versioning, Object Lock, lifecycle rules, bucket policies, IAM users and STS, and S3 Tables with a built-in Iceberg REST catalog. Everything ships in one `weed` binary, and `weed mini` runs all the roles in one process for a single node.
strengths: Fast with huge numbers of small files: one disk read per file and about 40 bytes of on-disk metadata each, where MinIO also writes a metadata file on every drive of the erasure set
Broad S3 support: versioning, Object Lock, lifecycle, bucket policies, IAM groups, STS with OIDC or LDAP, and SSE-S3, SSE-KMS and SSE-C
The same data as objects and as files, over S3, FUSE, WebDAV, SFTP, HDFS and a Kubernetes CSI driver
Grows by adding volume servers with no data reshuffle, and the filer and S3 gateways are stateless, so you run as many as you need
Apache 2.0, developed since 2011, with releases every week or two (4.48 in September 2026)
limits: No S3 bucket notification or bucket replication APIs and no S3 Select; cross-cluster replication and change events use SeaweedFS’s own replication and metadata feeds instead
More moving parts than MinIO: masters, volume servers, filers, a metadata database and S3 gateways, each with its own flags and failure modes
Missing replicas are not repaired automatically in normal operation: you run `volume.fix.replication`, balancing and vacuum from `weed shell` or the maintenance worker
Some data-safety features are Enterprise-only: self-healing storage, data recovery, point-in-time recovery and custom erasure coding ratios (open source is fixed at 10+4)
Heavily dependent on its founder: Chris Lu has written about two thirds of all commits

sections.title: Moving from MinIO
body: Copy data over the S3 API: rclone has a `SeaweedFS` provider setting, so `rclone sync minio:bucket seaweed:bucket` works, or use `mc mirror` if you still have the MinIO client. Run the sync again just before cutover, then switch endpoints. Users and policies have to be recreated; SeaweedFS manages them through AWS-style IAM calls rather than `mc admin`.

Plan around the gaps. Apps that react to MinIO bucket notifications need to subscribe to the filer’s metadata change events or webhooks instead, and MinIO bucket replication becomes SeaweedFS’s cluster-to-cluster replication. Unlike MinIO, SeaweedFS replicates new data first and erasure-codes it later, so size disks for the replication setting you choose.

story: In 2010 Facebook described Haystack, the system it built to store billions of photos. Ordinary file systems spent extra disk reads per photo on directory and inode metadata, so Haystack packed many photos into large files and kept a small index in memory, making each photo one disk read. In November 2011 Chris Lu started Weed-FS on Google Code, an open-source blob store in Go built on the same idea.

The project moved to GitHub, and in April 2015, after a user asked what it was actually called, Lu suggested “SeaweedFS”, keeping `weed` as the binary’s name. Over the following decade he added the filer with pluggable metadata stores, the S3 gateway, FUSE mounts, erasure coding for warm data inspired by Facebook’s later f4 paper, and cloud tiering.

Lu still writes most of the code, about two thirds of all commits, and funds the work through sponsors and a paid Enterprise edition. Versions 1.0, 3.0 and 4.0 came in 2018, 2022 and 2025, and the project now presents itself as one system for S3 objects, files and Iceberg tables.

choices.choice: Pack small files into big volume files
choices.why: Haystack showed that per-file metadata, not the data, was the bottleneck for photo serving. Appending files to large volumes with a tiny in-memory index turns every read into one disk seek.

choices.choice: The master tracks volumes, not files
choices.why: A cluster with billions of files has only thousands of volumes, so one master, or a Raft group of three, stays small and stays out of the read path.

choices.choice: Replicate hot data, erasure-code warm data
choices.why: Writing whole copies is fast. Sealing older volumes and converting them to 10+4 erasure coding later saves disk without making every write pay the encoding cost.

choices.choice: Keep directory metadata in an existing database
choices.why: Instead of writing its own metadata server, the filer stores names and directories in databases operators already run, from LevelDB to PostgreSQL, Redis and Cassandra.
